caseStudies.title: Messenger Archive & Semantic Search
caseStudies.problem: Long-running personal chat archives combine text and voice messages across thousands of threads, making keyword search ineffective for recalling context or supplying structured history to LLM agents.
caseStudies.context: Self-directed personal engineering project built independently outside employer work to explore Rust/Python interoperability, local speech-to-text, vector indexing, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tooling.
caseStudies.architecture: A Rust sync service fetches personal chat history over MTProto with flood-wait backoff into PostgreSQL. A Python worker claims pending voice rows using PostgreSQL FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (row-level locking that skips already locked rows) and transcribes them with Whisper. A Rust indexer computes batched local embeddings and upserts points into Qdrant, exposed to LLM agents via a read-only MCP server (stdio and HTTP).
challenges: No distributed transaction spans PostgreSQL, Qdrant, and the sync cursor checkpoint.
Coordinating concurrent transcription workers cleanly without blocking on rows currently claimed by another worker.
Respecting upstream MTProto rate limits while recovering from mid-batch interruptions.
decisions: Used PostgreSQL SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so concurrent workers take exclusive row-level locks on unclaimed tasks while skipping locked rows instead of waiting.
Computed deterministic UUIDv5 Qdrant point IDs from message identity so replay overwrites Qdrant entries idempotently instead of creating duplicates.
Persisted the indexing checkpoint only after each Qdrant upsert batch succeeds.
reliability: Provides at-least-once delivery across crashes; idempotent UUIDv5 upserts make Qdrant state convergent, whereas non-idempotent external side effects would require separate deduplication or compensating actions.
Does not claim end-to-end exactly-once processing across PostgreSQL and external consumers.
Flood-wait backoff and bounded retries protect upstream API sessions.
results: End-to-end personal archive searchable semantically across text and transcribed voice messages through read-only MCP tools.

caseStudies.title: EntityLocker — Row-Level Entity Concurrency Utility
caseStudies.problem: Single-JVM applications mutating or caching domain entities concurrently face either coarse global locks that bottleneck unrelated keys or ad-hoc per-key lock maps prone to deadlocks and memory growth.
caseStudies.context: Public open-source Java library (stden/EntityLocker) implementing JVM-local mutual exclusion comparable to per-row locking keyed by Comparable entity IDs.
caseStudies.architecture: A generic EntityLocker<T extends Comparable<T>> coordinator maintains a ConcurrentHashMap<T, CountLock> (a ReentrantLock subclass), supporting reentrant locking, millisecond acquisition timeouts via tryWithLock, and ascending Comparable ID ordering via ThreadLocal<T> for deadlock prevention among EntityLocker-managed locks within a single JVM process.
challenges: Isolating lock contention per entity ID within a single JVM without blocking unrelated keys.
Preventing lock-order deadlocks when a thread acquires multiple EntityLocker keys recursively.
Reclaiming idle lock entries without racing against concurrent computeIfAbsent acquisition or volatile counter updates.
decisions: Decoupled lock coordination from entity payload storage using generic Comparable<T> primary keys.
Enforced monotonic ascending lock ordering via ThreadLocal<T> tracking inside EntityLocker to reject out-of-order nested acquisitions.
Implemented tryWithLock timeouts and reentrant locking backed by JUnit concurrency, timeout, reentrancy, and deadlock-prevention tests.
reliability: Strictly JVM-local concurrency control (single process only; does not coordinate locks across multiple JVM instances or distributed nodes).
Deadlock prevention applies only to locks managed through the same EntityLocker instance, not external locks.

Implementation trade-off noted in code review: CountLock updates a volatile enters counter non-atomically and removes entries via remove(ID), so production high-cardinality use would need atomic ConcurrentHashMap.compute eviction and AtomicInteger tracking across both lock() and tryLock().
results: Published as a standalone reusable Java utility on GitHub (stden/EntityLocker) with JUnit 4 multithreaded tests.

architectureDiagrams.title: Semantic Search & MCP Integration
architectureDiagrams.label: Independent personal project architecture: MTProto sync service in Rust, PostgreSQL row-locked queue, Python Whisper worker, batched Rust indexer, Qdrant vector DB, and MCP server
architectureDiagrams.summary: Cross-language personal ingestion pipeline bridging PostgreSQL and Qdrant with at-least-once retries, idempotent UUIDv5 upserts, and read-only MCP tool exposure.

nodes.title: Messenger API (MTProto)
nodes.responsibility: Provides incremental message history and voice attachments subject to upstream rate limits.
nodes.tradeoffs: Rate-limited upstream API requires persistent cursor checkpoints to avoid costly full re-syncs.

nodes.title: Sync Service (Rust)
nodes.responsibility: Fetches history with exponential/flood-wait backoff and stores raw messages in PostgreSQL.
nodes.tradeoffs: Rust async runtime handles long-running sync sessions with predictable memory footprint.

nodes.title: PostgreSQL Store & Queue
nodes.responsibility: Stores canonical chat records and coordinates voice transcription jobs via row-level locks (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) so workers skip already locked rows.
nodes.tradeoffs: Row-level locking (not lock-free) removes an extra broker dependency at personal scale while requiring lease/timeout recovery if a worker dies mid-transaction.

nodes.title: Transcription Worker (Python)
nodes.responsibility: Claims untranscribed voice attachments under a database transaction and writes transcripts back to PostgreSQL.
nodes.tradeoffs: Separating Python ML execution keeps the core Rust sync and indexing paths lightweight.

nodes.title: Batch Indexer (Rust)
nodes.responsibility: Generates local text embeddings in batches and saves the indexing cursor only after Qdrant upsert confirmation.
nodes.tradeoffs: At-least-once checkpoint-after-upsert avoids distributed 2PC transactions across PostgreSQL and Qdrant.

nodes.title: Vector Store (Qdrant)
nodes.responsibility: Stores semantic embeddings keyed by deterministic UUIDv5 identifiers derived from message identity.
nodes.tradeoffs: Idempotent overwrites handle Qdrant retries safely, but do not extend automatically to non-idempotent external side effects.

nodes.title: MCP Server (stdio / HTTP)
nodes.responsibility: Exposes semantic search and thread retrieval tools to LLM assistants over Model Context Protocol.
nodes.tradeoffs: Read-only query tools isolate LLM agents from direct database or session credentials.

architectureDiagrams.title: JVM-Local Entity Concurrency Locking (EntityLocker)
architectureDiagrams.label: Open-source Java library EntityLocker: single-JVM caller threads, ConcurrentHashMap registry, per-ID CountLock (ReentrantLock), ThreadLocal ID-order check, and critical section
architectureDiagrams.summary: Public single-JVM Java concurrency utility providing per-ID mutual exclusion keyed by Comparable identifier without blocking unrelated keys.

nodes.title: JVM Caller Threads
nodes.responsibility: Threads inside a single JVM process request exclusive access to work identified solely by generic Comparable entity IDs.
nodes.tradeoffs: Strictly JVM-local synchronisation; multi-node services require database locks or an external distributed coordinator.

nodes.title: ConcurrentHashMap Registry
nodes.responsibility: Maps each active Comparable entity ID to a CountLock instance inside a ConcurrentHashMap.
nodes.tradeoffs: Hash-striped lookup avoids coarse global locking, though remove(ID) vs computeIfAbsent requires atomic compute() eviction under extreme churn.

nodes.title: CountLock (ReentrantLock)
nodes.responsibility: Provides reentrant per-ID mutual exclusion, millisecond tryWithLock timeouts, and ThreadLocal ascending ID ordering to prevent internal deadlocks.
nodes.tradeoffs: Ordering checks only cover locks acquired through EntityLocker; non-atomic enters counter in CountLock is a known trade-off in the public study.

nodes.title: Protected Critical Section
nodes.responsibility: Executes the guarded Runnable while holding only the target entity key lock.
nodes.tradeoffs: Short critical sections reduce per-key contention without serialising unrelated entity IDs.

nodes.title: Unlock & Map Cleanup
nodes.responsibility: Restores previous ThreadLocal maxLockedId, removes the map entry on outer release, and calls unlock().
nodes.tradeoffs: Bounding active map entries helps memory footprint, though lock-free remove() can race with concurrent threads acquiring the same key.

architectureDiagrams.originLabel: Independent educational reference architecture — unrelated to any employer system
architectureDiagrams.title: Transactional Outbox & Idempotent Consumer
architectureDiagrams.label: Educational reference architecture: application service, relational outbox transaction, outbox relay, message broker, idempotent consumer, and dead-letter queue
architectureDiagrams.summary: Standard educational distributed-systems pattern pairing atomic local outbox writes with at-least-once relay delivery and consumer-side deduplication.

nodes.title: Domain Service (Java / Spring)
nodes.responsibility: Validates incoming requests and executes domain state transitions inside a single local ACID transaction.
nodes.tradeoffs: Avoids brittle two-phase commit across database and message broker.

nodes.title: Relational DB + Outbox Table
nodes.responsibility: Persists domain state and outbox event payload in the same local database transaction.
nodes.tradeoffs: Ensures events are not lost on crash before publishing, at the cost of relational write amplification.

nodes.title: Outbox Relay Publisher
nodes.responsibility: Reads unpublished outbox rows and emits events to the message broker before marking rows published.
nodes.tradeoffs: Guarantees at-least-once delivery—not end-to-end exactly-once—because a crash after broker ack and before DB mark causes replay.

nodes.title: Message Broker (Kafka / AMQP)
nodes.responsibility: Decouples producers and consumers while buffering spikes and preserving per-key partition ordering.
nodes.tradeoffs: Partitioning scales throughput horizontally; ordering is per-partition rather than global.

nodes.title: Idempotent Consumer
nodes.responsibility: Records deterministic event IDs within the consumer transaction so redelivered events become safe no-ops for local state.
nodes.tradeoffs: Idempotency keys have retention/TTL limits and cannot automatically roll back non-idempotent third-party side effects.

nodes.title: Retry & Dead-Letter Queue
nodes.responsibility: Routes poison payloads after bounded backoff retries to a dead-letter queue for operator inspection.
nodes.tradeoffs: Prevents malformed messages from stalling healthy partition progress.

architectureDiagrams.originLabel: Independent educational reference architecture — unrelated to any employer system
architectureDiagrams.title: Resilient Asynchronous Job Queue & Backpressure
architectureDiagrams.label: Educational reference architecture: API producer, persistent job queue with row-level locks, bounded worker pool, atomic result staging, and observability metrics
architectureDiagrams.summary: Standard educational pattern decoupling slow background jobs from synchronous API latency using bounded worker pools and safe retries.

nodes.title: Stateless API Frontend
nodes.responsibility: Authenticates requests, enqueues work asynchronously, and returns a job correlation ID immediately.
nodes.tradeoffs: Keeps request threads fast and predictable instead of blocking on long-running background work.

nodes.title: Persistent Work Queue
nodes.responsibility: Durably tracks queued, in-flight, completed, and failed job states with lease/visibility timeouts.
nodes.tradeoffs: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED uses row-level exclusive locks while skipping locked rows; lease timeouts enable at-least-once recovery after worker crashes.

nodes.title: Bounded Worker Pool
nodes.responsibility: Executes tasks up to a configured concurrency ceiling to protect downstream CPU, memory, and DB connection pools.
nodes.tradeoffs: Backpressure caps queue drain rate to prevent cascading overload.

nodes.title: Staged Write & Atomic Commit
nodes.responsibility: Writes output artifacts to staging before committing job completion so readers never observe partial output.
nodes.tradeoffs: Crashed workers leave orphaned staging files that require scheduled TTL cleanup.

nodes.title: Health, Metrics & Cleanup
nodes.responsibility: Exports queue lag, retry counts, and purges expired staging artifacts on a predictable schedule.
nodes.tradeoffs: Scheduled TTL cleanup decouples storage reclamation from user-facing latency.

engineeringConcepts.name: Idempotency & Its Limits
engineeringConcepts.description: Deterministic UUIDv5 vector point IDs and consumer deduplication tables prevent duplicate state on retries, though deduplication stores require bounded TTLs and external side effects need separate safeguards.

engineeringConcepts.name: At-Least-Once vs Exactly-Once
engineeringConcepts.description: Transactional outbox relays and durable queues guarantee at-least-once delivery rather than automatic end-to-end exactly-once processing; idempotent consumers reconcile duplicate deliveries.

engineeringConcepts.name: Eventual Consistency
engineeringConcepts.description: Advancing sync checkpoints only after downstream upserts succeed and committing outbox rows alongside domain state keeps separate data stores convergent.

engineeringConcepts.name: Row-Level Locking & JVM Locks
engineeringConcepts.description: PostgreSQL FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED uses row-level exclusive locks while skipping locked rows across workers; EntityLocker provides single-JVM per-key ReentrantLock synchronisation.

engineeringConcepts.name: Failure Handling & Backpressure
engineeringConcepts.description: Bounded worker pools, exponential flood-wait backoff, lease timeouts, and dead-letter queues keep transient failures recoverable without cascading overload.

engineeringConcepts.name: Observability
engineeringConcepts.description: Queue lag metrics, explicit job state machines, dead-letter alerts, and automated quality-gate checks (SonarQubeChecker) keep faults diagnosable.

engineeringConcepts.name: Security
engineeringConcepts.description: Least-privilege read-only MCP interfaces, stateless API input validation, and isolating runtime credentials away from AI agent tool surfaces.
